extracted.intended_audience: IGCSE First Language English students preparing for Paper 2 (narrative)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and the mark-scheme criteria for Cambridge IGCSE First Language English Paper 2 Section B (narrative writing), including what examiners look for and exam-time techniques to produce a high-scoring story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and Accuracy (24 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Precise, well-chosen vocabulary and varied sentence structures, chosen for effect; consistent well-chosen register suitable for the context; spelling, punctuation, and grammar almost always accurate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dimension rewards language control and craft: select vocabulary deliberately for effect, vary sentence types and lengths, maintain an appropriate and consistent register, and aim for near-perfect mechanics (spelling, punctuation, grammar). Examiners allocate 24 marks to this area; lapses in accuracy or inappropriate register reduce the score here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and Structure (16 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The plot is well-defined and strongly developed with features of fiction writing such as description characterization and effective climax and convincing details."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion focuses on narrative organisation and substance: a clear, developed plot with a beginning, middle and end; effective pacing and climax; purposeful descriptive passages; believable characterisation and convincing, specific details that support the story. Examiners allocate 16 marks to content and structure; weak development, thin plotting, or lack of convincing detail lowers the mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to the narrative genre and task
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the student chooses to write in response to the Narrative prompt, it’s essential to stick to narrative writing. This is because the rubric varies from Descriptive to Narrative, and the Narrative rubric looks for specific features of narrative writing: a plot with a beginning, middle, and end; well-described characters; and strong, convincing details."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a prompt intended for narrative responses and ensure your piece is a story (not an informative/report-style answer). Failing to meet the genre expectation (e.g., turning a narrative prompt into an informative piece) means the piece will be judged against the wrong criteria and lose marks. Focus on telling a coherent story with narrative techniques rather than explaining or describing non-narratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding accurately to prompt-specific requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompts may require specific constraints (e.g., end with a given phrase, include particular words, use a title or involve a particular situation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure you satisfy any explicit instructions in the prompt (include the required phrase/title, handle the stated circumstance). Use the most specific elements of the prompt to build your plot. Failure to incorporate required elements can cost marks or make your response irrelevant to the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam technique: planning, focus, and handling writer’s block
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice: build around the prompt that provides the most specific information; concentrate on one main event, one or two characters, and a distinct problem with a solution; create a concise outline (beginning, middle, end) before writing; recycle and adapt practiced stories if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These production-focused criteria improve execution under exam conditions. A short plan helps structure the plot and avoid losing focus. Limiting scope (single main event, few characters) helps develop convincing detail and a clear climax. Practising and adapting pre-written story frameworks can be an effective exam strategy. Repeated practice and teacher feedback are recommended to internalise these techniques.
